newsitem.title: MEXICO: Mexico says must fight rebels first, poverty later.
newsitem.headline: Mexico says must fight rebels first, poverty later.

text.p: The Mexican government said on Thursday that it must defeat "terrorism" by a new leftist guerrilla group before it can address the extreme poverty that critics say helped spawn it.

"I am not being an apologist for the existence of poor people in Mexico; anyone who does is blind and ethically irresponsible," Interior Minister Emilio Chuayffet said in testimony to the Mexican Congress.
"Nevertheless, not even poverty justifies terrorism."

President Ernesto Zedillo, in his second State of the Nation speech on Sept. 1, pledged to apply "the full force of the State" against the Popular Revolutionary Army (EPR), which first appeared in June and launched attacks against the army and police in several states last month.

Asked by opposition legislators why the State was not instead bringing its full force to bear against poverty, which they said helped breed guerrilla movements, Chuayffet replied: "If we do not apply it, terrorism destroys the State and then you have no force to apply against poverty."
Juan Sanchez Navarro, a frequent critic of the government who is seen by many as the intellectual spokesman of Mexico's private sector, disagreed.

"When you reach the extreme limit of poverty, everything is valid," the millionaire head of beer giant Modelo said after a meeting of business leaders. He added that the Dec. 1994 peso crisis and ensuing recession had stalled necessary democratic reforms in Mexico.

In a speech Thursday in the central state of San Luis Potosi, Zedillo urged poor peasant farmers to shun arms and promised the government would hand over some 74,000 acres (30,000 hectares) of land to them in the next two years.
"We Mexicans do not need other weapons, because we have those given to us by the law and democracy," Zedillo said.
The EPR is believed to have a presence in the mountainous Huasteca region that covers part of San Luis Potosi state, as well as in a handful of other southern and central states.

The government of the southern state of Oaxaca, where the EPR carried out several fierce attacks in August, meanwhile, released an artist's impression of an EPR leader it is seeking, named as Alejandro Constantino Canseco Ruiz.
In the nearby state of Tabasco, one of four alleged EPR members held for taking part in a radio station seizure was freed on bail.
About 20 alleged EPR members were under arrest in various parts of the country. Some have alleged torture by police.

The EPR, in a statement carried by Excelsior newspaper on Thursday, accused the government of using dirty tricks, including the dissemination of false information and threats in its name to try and discredit it.

"These manoeuvres are part of the disinformation and psychological war campaign deployed by the State against us in order to create confusion and discredit us in the eyes of the population," said the statement, which the newspaper said was left at a location in Mexico City for Excelsior to collect.
The EPR denied carrying out a recent spate of bomb threats in several Mexican cities.

The government, which draws a sharp distinction between the EPR and the country's Zapatista rebels in the southern state of Chiapas, said it believed suspended peace talks with the Zapatistas could be revived.
"A dignified peace, with neither winners nor losers, is possible," Chuayffet said.
Zapatista leader Subcommander Marcos broke off talks on Sept. 2, saying the government was not negotiating seriously.
Mediators on Thursday released a document in which they urged further confidence-building measures by the two sides.
Business leaders also published paid advertisements in a Mexico City newspaper on Thursday urging the Zapatistas to return to the negotiating table.
